summary.title: Human error: models and management
summary.one_liner: Learn the two models of human error, the person approach and the system approach, and why they lead to different ways of managing risk in clinical practice.
takeaways: Human error can be framed as a person approach (blame individuals for forgetfulness, carelessness or recklessness) or a system approach (errors are consequences of upstream systemic factors).

The person approach relies on fear campaigns, procedures, discipline and retraining, and tends to treat errors as moral issues; the article argues it is ill suited to medicine and can block safer institutions.
The system approach accepts that humans are fallible and focuses on changing working conditions and building barriers and safeguards, asking how and why defences failed rather than who blundered.
Effective risk management depends on a reporting culture that analyses mishaps, incidents and near misses to find recurrent error traps.
High reliability organisations treat human variability as something to harness and stay preoccupied with the possibility of failure.
summary.summary: This short BMJ education and debate article by James Reason, a psychology professor, contrasts the person approach and the system approach to human error. It describes how each model explains error causation and what management responses follow from it. The article then evaluates the person approach, noting that most errors in areas like aviation maintenance are blameless and that reporting cultures are essential to risk management. It closes with summary points on high reliability organisations.
